designs.title: How Beer Is Made
designs.why: Clean, consistent line work, and it prints cleanly in one ink on black. But it reads like a brewery-tour handout or textbook diagram, not apparel. Seven boxes with arrows and a generic geometric sans make an evenly weighted grid with no hero. From 3 m it's a grey rectangle of small icons. The one-line captions are too small to read on a back and turn the shirt into homework. Hard to justify at $50.
designs.fix: Cut the captions and give it a hero: one large brew kettle in the middle with the other steps as small numbered vignettes around it, and a heading with real character (condensed or hand-lettered) instead of the default tracked sans.

designs.title: Gin Botanicals
designs.why: The strongest of the three. Antique botanical-plate language, with the italic Latin names giving it authority. Five specimens are balanced in a loose grid with good negative space, and the silhouettes read from distance. On a white tee it feels like a considered heritage graphic that can carry $50. Close up, the halftone is a little coarse and gritty in the darker roots and peel, and the layout is a touch static.
designs.fix: Open up the halftone in the dense dark areas (or move to engraved line hatching) so the roots and peel stay crisp instead of gritty, and tighten the bottom row so the orris root and petals sit as one locked unit.

designs.title: Vineyard
designs.why: From 3 m it reads well: the arched window, spaced grotesk heading and keyline give a calm, quiet structure, and the terraced vineyard sitting inside it on a white tee looks clean. Up close the problems show. The 'engraving' is really a 1–2 px dither or stochastic halftone at 300 DPI, roughly 85–170 micron dots. On a single screen on cotton that will plug in the dark leaves and cypresses and drop out across the pale distant hills and walls, so the print will look muddy and patchy, not crisp. Some areas are already mushy: the house, the vine rows and the far hills read as grey noise, not cut lines. The scene is also generic Tuscan postcard art, with nothing that makes it ours, which is thin for a $50 tee.
designs.fix: Rebuild the art for the screen. Turn the fine dither into true engraved line work, or at least a coarse halftone (about 40–45 lpi) with a minimum dot that holds and the light tones knocked out cleanly. That keeps the grapes, house and terraces crisp on press, not muddy.
